sentences[0].why: A yes/no question folded into a sentence starts with ob — 'whether'.

help.intro: An indirect question wraps a question inside a polite opener — Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist? Wissen Sie, ob das Geschäft offen ist? — and it is the politest way to ask anything in German, which is why you will hear it at every counter, on every phone call and at every information desk. The grammar is the subordinate-clause rule you already have from weil and dass: the question becomes a clause with the verb at the end. A W-question keeps its W-word (wo, wann, wie, warum, was, wer); a yes/no question gets ob (whether). The openers are few: Können / Könnten Sie mir sagen, …? · Wissen Sie, …? · Weißt du, …? · Ich weiß nicht, … · Ich möchte wissen, …
help.tips[0].title: W-question → W-word + verb at the end
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: Could you tell me how I get to the museum?
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: Do you know when the film starts?
help.tips[0].trap: 'Können Sie mir sagen, wo ist der Bahnhof?' keeps the direct order. Inside the opener, the verb goes last.
help.tips[0].check.why: Inside the polite opener the question becomes a subordinate clause: W-word, subject, verb at the end — wo die Post ist.
help.tips[1].title: Yes/no question → ob + verb at the end
help.tips[1].text: Ist das Geschäft offen? → Wissen Sie, ob das Geschäft offen ist? Kommt er? → Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. ob = whether / if.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: Do you know whether she has time today?
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: I don't know whether I can come tomorrow.
help.tips[1].check.q: Weißt du, ____ der Supermarkt sonntags offen ist? (Do you know whether …)
help.tips[1].check.why: A yes/no question has no W-word, so it is wrapped with ob (whether). wenn never means 'whether'.
help.tips[2].title: The openers
help.tips[2].text: Können Sie mir sagen, …? (can you tell me) · Wissen Sie / Weißt du, …? · Ich weiß nicht, … · Ich möchte wissen, … · Ich frage mich, … (I wonder). The comma comes after the opener.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: I'd like to know how much that costs.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: I wonder why he isn't calling.
help.tips[2].check.q: Ich ____ mich, warum der Bus heute so spät kommt. (I wonder why …)
help.tips[2].check.why: 'I wonder' is the opener Ich frage mich, … — followed by a comma and the clause with the verb at the end.
help.tips[3].title: Politeness by wrapping
help.tips[3].text: Wo ist die Toilette? is fine with friends. Könnten Sie mir sagen, wo die Toilette ist? is how you ask a stranger. Same question, wrapped.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: Excuse me, could you tell me where there's a bank here?
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: Do you know what time it is?
help.tips[3].check.q: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie mir sagen, wann ____?
help.tips[3].check.why: The polite wrapping changes the word order: the verb öffnet moves to the end and still agrees with das Museum.
help.remember[0]: Wrap the question: opener + comma + W-word/ob + … + verb last.
help.context.en: Excuse me, can you tell me where the main station is? – Straight on, then left. – And do you know whether a café is open there? – I think so. – Could you also tell me when the next train to Cologne leaves? – I'm afraid I don't know. Ask at the counter whether there's a train at ten.
help.mistakes[0].why: In the indirect question the verb goes to the end.
help.hook: Ask strangers anything, politely: wrap your question in 'Können Sie mir sagen, …?' and send the verb to the end.
